participation.text: State institutions, occupation and collaboration enabled systematic persecution; responses varied.

evidence.text: Documents and individual testimony must be read together; a total is not a biography.

name: War, occupation and genocide
place: Europe, Asia and wider war zones; locator at Berlin
geographicPrecision: Nazi state-capital anchor; persecution and war extended far beyond it. No locator implies all victims lived here.

interval.label: Persecution 1933–1945; wider war contexts 1937/1939–1945
interval.note: Holocaust frame differs from war chronology: Japanese expansion inChina precedes European war in 1939. Not a single universal start for all regions.

question: How did institutions turn prejudice and conquest into persecution and mass murder?
summary: Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators persecuted and murdered six million European Jews in the Holocaust. Other groups were also targeted. War and occupation extended state violence across regions. This history requires attention to victims’ lives, decisions and institutions, rather than treating suffering as an anonymous total.

sections.title: Distinguish connected chronologies
sections.text: USHMM dates the Holocaust 1933–1945. Its war account describes Japan’s 1931 Manchurian conquest and 1937 invasion of China, and Germany’s September 1939 invasion of Poland. These histories connect, but an atlas should not erase earlier Asian warfare to fit one European date.

citations.locator: German and Japanese Expansion; Invasion of Poland

sections.title: Name the crime accurately
sections.text: The Holocaust was a systematic, state-sponsored persecution and genocide of European Jews by the Nazi regime, its allies and collaborators. Discrimination and exclusion intensified into mass murder. The museum also documents persecution and murder of other groups; their histories should not be erased or collapsed into one undifferentiated category.

citations.locator: Definition, key facts and other victims

sections.title: People were more than their persecution
sections.text: The museum’s individual histories and testimony offer ways to study lives and choices beyond a statistic. Its account distinguishes perpetrators, collaborators, bystanders and people who resisted or helped. A serious explanation asks how institutions and decisions enabled violence without claiming it was inevitable.

citations.locator: Who was responsible; Jewish responses and rescue discussion

sections.title: Ginling’s workers prepared rooms and disagreed about safety
sections.text: Ginling College in Nanjing was already a place of education when Japanese invasion made its campus part of civilian refuge. In her 6 December 1937 diary, Minnie Vautrin described Mr Chen and Mr Li directing furniture into an attic and preparing buildings. She still needed to decide how space would be assigned. Her 15 December entry describes a long day at the gate admitting refugees. Rooms, bedding, food and time mattered alongside an announced place of safety. Tsen Shui-fang, a Chinese colleague, kept her own diary. The consulted English excerpt for 21 December records her distrust of promised protection and her concern about reports to Japanese officials. That is her dated judgment, not Vautrin’s voice and not a statement about every Japanese person. In a 4 January 1938 letter, Vautrin described sharing campus rounds with Mary after Mrs Tsen and she persuaded Mary to stay. The letter also describes disrupted communication. These records document effort under danger. They do not prove that a campus boundary made anyone secure. An estimate of a crowd is not a census.

citations.locator: 6 December 1937, printed p. 97; 15 December 1937, printed p. 111

sections.title: A card, a passbook and a recollection answer different questions
sections.text: In occupied Singapore, household registration supported ration cards. The published provisions-card caption names cereal, soap, matches and meat and expressly excludes rice, sugar and salt. That is an administrative entitlement, not proof of a meal. The National Archives of Singapore describes a passbook of Lee Hiok Khuang, in the Lee Siew Hong collection, with deposits dated 1944 and 1945. A deposit is a transaction, not a complete household budget. Lee Tian Soo later recalled keeping chickens as a student in Chinatown and looking for feed when scraps were scarce. The National Library Board publishes that excerpt from an interview recorded on 14 May 1983. The page used here was published in 2019. The recollection is one person’s memory. It is not a wartime diary, and the original interview was not read.

citations.locator: Provisions-card caption; Lee Tian Soo excerpt and endnote 17
On Inflation; passbook deposits dated 1944 and 1945

sections.title: A named writer asked that his family be remembered
sections.text: Izrael Lichtensztajn taught and wrote children’s stories before the war. In a testament dated 31 July 1942 he asked that his wife, the painter Gela Seksztajn, and their daughter be remembered. Dawid Graber’s 3 August 1942 text describes gathering and burying evidence during deportation. Emanuel Ringelblum’s personal chronicle is dated from October 1939, and organized archive work followed the sealing of the Warsaw ghetto in November 1940. The English passages used here are a selected 2019 rendering by Olga Drenda for the Jewish Historical Institute, not the manuscripts. A request shows this writer’s relationships and purpose. It does not stand for every Jewish experience, and it does not show that the writers knew the future.

citations.locator: Lichtensztajn, 31 July 1942; Graber, 3 August 1942; translation by Olga Drenda

deeperReading.title: Keep the speaker, the date and the version apart
deeperReading.text: Vautrin’s diary and letter have wartime dates. Their digital copies do not make an upload date a historical event. The English Tsen passage is a selected translation from a 2010 edition, on a page dated 2018. Her Chinese manuscript and that whole volume were not read. Lee Tian Soo’s words were recorded in 1983 and published as an excerpt in 2019. The original National Archives of Singapore interview remains unread, and the card and passbook images were not inspected. Lichtensztajn’s testament is dated 31 July 1942. The consulted English is Drenda’s 2019 translation. Graber’s text reports a 20 July start for the deportation he describes, while the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives 22 July. Both dates stay as the sources state them. None of these versions supplies an unread manuscript.

deeperReading.title: What each record lets us ask
deeperReading.text: At Ginling, a diary and a letter show how people organized shelter and disagreed about safety. Reading the translated excerpts leaves some of Tsen’s wording and context beyond reach. In Singapore, a household card lists provisions, while a later interview recalls someone’s experience. To find out what a household actually received, we would need evidence of distribution. In Warsaw, people chose what to collect and bury so that others could learn about lives under persecution. Ask who created each record, who could use it and what the people who made it hoped would follow.

evidenceReading.title: Work, entitlement and a request to be remembered
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of consulted records. Do not invent a diary, act out refuge or persecution, or compare suffering.

items.label: Preparing space at Ginling
items.text: Vautrin’s 6 December 1937 diary describes Mr Chen and Mr Li moving furniture and preparing buildings. Her 15 December entry describes a day at the gate admitting refugees.
items.interpretation: The diary establishes particular work in progress. It does not measure the campus, count every refugee or prove that the place was safe.

citations.locator: 6 December 1937, printed p. 97; 15 December 1937, printed p. 111

items.label: Tsen Shui-fang’s judgment
items.text: The translated excerpt for 21 December 1937 records Tsen’s distrust of promised protection.
items.interpretation: Name the speaker, the occupation circumstance and the later English version. Do not merge her judgment with Vautrin’s. The Chinese original was not read.

items.label: Shared rounds after the new year
items.text: Vautrin’s 4 January 1938 letter describes sharing campus rounds with Mary.
items.interpretation: The work continued across days and depended on several people. Effort is not proof that protection succeeded.

items.label: A provisions card is not a meal
items.text: The published caption identifies a household purchasing card and lists goods it excludes, including rice, sugar and salt.
items.interpretation: The caption describes an entitlement. It does not establish what was bought. The card image was not inspected.

items.label: One passbook and one memory
items.text: The archives describe 1944 and 1945 deposits in Lee Hiok Khuang’s passbook. Lee Tian Soo’s published excerpt recalls keeping chickens. The interview was recorded on 14 May 1983.
items.interpretation: A transaction and a later recollection have different purposes. Neither is a wartime diary or a survey of Singapore households. The original interview was not read.

items.label: Lichtensztajn’s request
items.text: On 31 July 1942 Izrael Lichtensztajn asked that his wife, Gela Seksztajn, and their daughter be remembered.
items.interpretation: The request is this writer’s act. The consulted English is Olga Drenda’s 2019 translation. It does not speak for every Jewish experience, and it is not permission to invent the testimony that was not read.

citations.locator: Lichtensztajn, 31 July 1942; translation by Olga Drenda

familyActivity.title: Read the source capsules with an adult
familyActivity.duration: About 15 minutes, for an older reader
steps: Do this with an adult. Do not act out refuge, occupation, hunger or persecution, and do not write an imagined diary or testament.
From the Ginling capsules, name the speaker on 6 December 1937, 21 December 1937 and 4 January 1938. Write one thing that record can establish and one thing it cannot.
Separate the Singapore provisions card, the 1944–1945 passbook deposits and Lee Tian Soo’s 1983 recollection. Explain why permission to purchase is not proof of a meal.
Read Lichtensztajn’s 31 July 1942 request in the 2019 English rendering. State who he asks to be remembered, then mark one question the rendering cannot answer.
familyActivity.explanation: Vautrin records preparation and shared campus rounds. Tsen’s translated excerpt questions promised protection. The Singapore card states an entitlement that excludes rice, sugar and salt. The passbook records deposits. Lee Tian Soo’s chicken-keeping is a memory recorded in 1983. Lichtensztajn asks that Gela Seksztajn and their daughter be remembered. These are particular records. They are not a young child’s activity, a role to play or a complete history of Nanjing, Singapore or Warsaw.

review.scope: Bounded explanations and source capsules for Ginling, Singapore household records and the Oneg Shabbat testament, placed on world-war-two. The original 1933–1945 interval, identity, claims, objectIds and comparison dimensions stay in place. No regional dossier was added.
